name: Affiliate widgets & marketplaces
headline: Widget-driven solar marketing and affiliate networks
summary: Not every financing path starts with a lender API. Affinity partners, publishers, and utilities embed calculators and prequal widgets — then earn CPA or revenue share when a homeowner requests quotes or signs a contract.

key_facts.label: Embed style
key_facts.value: HTML/JS snippets and iframes — little or no backend work

key_facts.label: Tracking
key_facts.value: Cookies, referral parameters, session attribution to commission

key_facts.label: Homeowner cue
key_facts.value: You may be on a partner site long before an installer calls

sections.heading: EnergySage’s widget model
sections.body: EnergySage — often called the “Kayak of solar,” backed by Schneider Electric — runs a large U.S. online marketplace and a structured partner program for nonprofits, corporates, and utilities. Partners embed savings calculators, community solar search maps, and educational libraries. Interaction attaches a tracking parameter; if you later request quotes and contract through the marketplace, the partner earns a negotiated commission or a sustainability KPI.

sections.heading: Why widgets beat raw lead APIs for partners
sections.body: Iframe/JS embeds bypass partner-side API auth, PII routing, and much of the compliance overhead of handling credit data. Organizations with limited IT can still publish a “[State] solar cost calculator” that ranks for SEO and captures high-intent leads.

sections.heading: Prequal widgets on installer sites
sections.body: Marketplaces like Acorn Finance optimize for top-of-funnel conversion: anonymous visitors run a soft-pull prequalification before talking to sales. Approved loan amounts flow into the contractor CRM so outreach starts with verified buying power. That is different from EnergySage’s multi-installer auction, but the embed pattern is similar.

sections.heading: Traditional CPA and revenue-share networks
sections.body: Independent publishers and review sites often monetize with banner creatives and parameterized affiliate URLs rather than interactive calculators. A custom “California Solar Payback Calculator” might be fully hand-coded, then send outbound traffic through tracking links. Disclosures should still be obvious when content is sponsored.

sections.heading: Widget types you will see
sections.body: Common embeds include zip + utility-bill savings calculators, community solar map search for renters, slide-to-estimate loan term calculators, “as low as $/mo” microcopy on invoices, and prequalify CTAs that open a modal soft-pull flow.

questions_to_ask: If I came through a calculator widget, am I locked into one marketplace’s installer network?
Who receives my contact info, and can I get cash quotes outside the affiliate path?
Is the publisher paid per lead, per contract, or via revenue share?
red_flags: “Independent” review site with no affiliate disclosure.
Calculator that only outputs a phone form — no assumptions shown.
Prequal widget that is unclear about soft vs hard credit pull.

faqs.question: Are affiliate marketplace quotes worse than direct installer quotes?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — competition can help — but you should still normalize $/W, separate batteries, and compare at least one independent cash quote. See our quote check tool.

faqs.question: Why do utilities embed EnergySage-style tools?
faqs.answer: They get a trusted educational surface and measurable program engagement without building a full lending stack or installer CRM.
